title: The Two Sorrows of the Luminaries and the Joy at the End
arc: The teaching opens by saying that no man — and indeed not even the great luminaries, the sun and moon — rejoices wholly in the present cosmos, because two corruptions are visible from their fixed station: the enemy enthroned where he does not belong, and the Living Soul afflicted and transmigrated body to body; and it ends by promising that when the soul is redeemed and the enemy bound at the consummation, this grief will give way to permanent joy.
reading:
This chapter takes up a quiet but profound paradox: the most stable, most exalted things in the visible cosmos — the sun and moon, "the luminaries of the heavens" — nevertheless do not rejoice wholly. They are introduced precisely as that which "stands on its feet" and "lasts forth until the end," figures of what is permanent in a world that is itself fragile. They cast no shadow and "do not know" what shadow is; they belong to the order of pure manifestation, Divine Truth in its illuminating and reflective registers. And yet, the master says, even they bear grief upon their heart. The teaching is built to show why.

The cause of their incomplete joy is twofold, and the doubling is the heart of the chapter. On the one hand, "their eyes gaze upon their enemy" — they see the King of Darkness sitting in a place that does not befit him, "arrogant, his heart at rest in a wealth that befits him not." This is the first corruption visible to the luminaries: the proprium ruling as though it were a true king, occupying a throne not its own, having stolen the appearance of dominion. The natural mind, which ought to be governed by Divine Truth, is presently held in a counterfeit kingship; the luminaries see this counterfeit every time they look down. On the other hand — and this is the deeper grief — they "are filled after the Living Soul." Wherever they shine, they perceive Divine Truth dispersed and suffering in the natural: drawn taut, set "above and below, in the tree and the thorn," oppressed in every affliction, torn and devoured, moving "from above to below, from below to above," plundered and "transferred forth from body to body." This is the cosmic Cross of Light read through the eyes of the luminaries: the soul they love, honored before them, is the one they watch being eaten by the proprium and shuttled through metensomatosis.

So the chapter sets up two registers of corruption that the cosmos suffers and that the heavenly witnesses see: a false enthronement above (the enemy as illegitimate king-face) and a captive dispersal below (the Living Soul wandering body to body). Between these two, the sun and moon stand fast. Their steadiness is not indifference; they are vigilant watchers, doing every work that pleases the Father "according to his heart's desire," operating "in a hidden way and a release-forth" both in the upper place and the lower. They are agents of the Call (ⲧⲱⲍⲙⲉ) — they stand on their feet "in a summons-forth" — but their work is not yet finished, and they know it.

What is permanent, then, in this teaching, is not yet joy but station. The luminaries are stationed witnesses; their fixity is a kind of patience, like Omophoros or the Holder, bearing the weight of a still-mingled cosmos. Their grief is precisely the measure of their love: they grieve because they love the soul that is "beloved before them and honored by them," and they grieve because they cannot abide the spectacle of a false king sitting where Divine Truth alone has the right to rule.

The arc closes by naming the resolution. They will not rejoice in completion until two things happen, and these two answer exactly to the two grievings. First, they will "redeem the Living Soul and bring her out from under the claws of the enemy" — the dispersed truth gathered home, the metensomatosis ended. Second, they will "release her forth from Death" and "bind their enemy in the bond at the end" — the false king deposed and fixed in his proper place, the bolos sealed. Only then, the chapter says, will they rejoice and "not give ear to grief any more from this moment," abiding "in their condition, that very condition" forever. The "condition" is the steady stationing they already have; what changes is that grief is taken out of it. The permanent thing in the cosmos becomes, at the consummation, also the joyful thing.

Read as one movement, the teaching is a meditation on why even the highest natural manifestations of Divine Truth — sun and moon, the two ships of light — share the suffering of the redemption process. They are not exempt observers; they are participants whose joy is bound to the outcome of the cosmic war. The chapter teaches the reader to see his own state in theirs: anyone who truly stands in the light cannot rejoice wholly while the proprium still rules where it ought not and while Divine Truth still suffers in mingled natural states. The promise at the end is that this conjoined grief is the very thing that will be transformed into conjoined joy when the soul is raised and the enemy bound.
